title: What is a pull request, and how to open one on GitHub
summary: A pull request asks to merge one branch into another after review. Learn its parts, its path from draft to merge, and how to open one on GitHub.
body_markdown:
A pull request (PR) is a proposal to merge changes from one branch into another, on a page where teammates read the diff, discuss it and see automated check results before anything merges. GitHub[calls the pull request](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/pull-requests) its key collaboration feature, the place to discuss and review changes before merging them.


## What a pull request is


The idea is older than GitHub. Git ships a`[git request-pull](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-request-pull)` command that generates "a request asking your upstream project to pull changes into their tree," and Linux kernel maintainers still[send pull requests](https://docs.kernel.org/maintainer/pull-requests.html) to each other by email. A pull request on GitHub makes the same request on a web page that holds the diff, the discussion, the reviews and the check results.


GitHub's own[glossary](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/github-glossary) says a pull request "can be thought of as a request to merge," and GitLab names the same feature a merge request.[Pull request vs merge request](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/pull-request-vs-merge-request) compares how GitHub and GitLab handle drafts, approvals, merge methods and merge trains.


A pull request is also different from a commit. A commit is a saved change to one or more files, which git records with a unique ID (its SHA). A pull request groups the commits on one branch and asks to merge them into another, so it usually holds several commits, and you can keep adding commits after you open it.


## The parts of a pull request


Part


What it is


Base branch


The branch your changes merge into, often` main`


Head branch


The branch that holds your commits, also called the compare branch


Commits


The commits on the head branch that make up the change


Diff


Every line added, changed or removed


Title and description


What the change does, why, and which issues it closes


Reviewers and reviews


Who was asked to review, and what each reviewer decided


Checks


CI builds, tests and other automated validations


Merge status


What still blocks the merge, such as missing approvals or failing checks


GitHub lays these out in tabs. Conversation holds the description, timeline, comments and reviews. Commits shows how the branch changed over time, Checks shows the automated results, and Files changed shows the diff that reviewers read. A Findings tab shows automated results such as code scanning alerts. The merge status appears in the pull request header and in the merge box.


### Branches


Pull requests can only be opened between two different branches. When everyone on a team can push to the repository, the head branch lives in that same repository, which GitHub calls the shared repository model. Open source projects often use the fork and pull model instead, where contributors fork the repository and open the pull request from a branch in their fork.


### Title and description


The description explains the change to people who weren't there when you wrote it. It can also close issues. If the description says` Fixes #123` and the pull request targets the default branch, GitHub[links issue 123](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue) and closes it when the pull request merges. The keywords are close, closes, closed, fix, fixes, fixed, resolve, resolves and resolved, and GitHub ignores them when the pull request targets any other branch.


A[pull request template](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/pull-request-template) pre-fills every new description with the sections your team expects, such as what changed and why, how it was tested, and the risk.


## The life of a pull request


### Draft


A draft pull request is for work in progress that you want to share without formally asking for review. Drafts can't be merged, and GitHub doesn't automatically request reviews from code owners while a pull request is a draft.


### Ready for review


When the work is done, click **Ready for review** in the merge box, or run` gh pr ready` . Marking it ready[requests reviews](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/create-pull-requests/changing-the-stage-of-a-pull-request) from any code owners. You can convert a pull request back to a draft at any time, for example after feedback that needs more work, and nobody can merge it until it's marked ready again.


### Review


Request reviews from the sidebar. With write access to the repository, you can[ask any person or team](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/create-pull-requests/requesting-a-pull-request-review) with read access to it, and GitHub suggests reviewers based on git blame data. If the repository has a CODEOWNERS file, GitHub requests reviews from the owners of the code a pull request changes. The[CODEOWNERS guide](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/codeowners) covers how to map paths to owners so the right reviewers are asked automatically.


Each[review](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/pull-request-reviews) ends with one of three decisions:


-


**Comment** : general feedback, without approving or requesting changes.


-


**Approve** : the changes are ready to merge.


-


**Request changes** : feedback the author should address before merging.


Two details catch people out. Request changes is informational on its own, and it only blocks merging when a ruleset or branch protection rule requires a pull request before merging. And[authors can't approve](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/review-pull-requests/approving-a-pull-request-with-required-reviews) their own pull requests.


Admins can go further and[protect a branch](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches) so that every pull request needs a set number of approving reviews, optionally including one from a code owner. They can also dismiss approvals when new commits change the diff, or require the most recent push to be approved by someone other than the person who pushed it.


For what a good review checks, see[what code review is](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/what-is-code-review) . For the clicks involved, see[how to review a pull request on GitHub](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/how-to-review-a-pull-request-on-github) .


### Status checks


[Status checks](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/status-checks) show whether a pull request's commits meet the conditions set for the repository. They usually come from external systems such as CI builds, tests, code scanning or deployments. GitHub Actions and other GitHub Apps create checks with detailed output and annotations, and other services can post simpler commit statuses.


If a branch requires status checks, they have to pass before the pull request can merge. One gotcha from GitHub's docs: a skipped job reports its status as "Success," so it won't block a merge even when it's a required check. To follow checks from a terminal, run` gh pr checks --watch` .


### Merge


You need write permission to merge, and drafts can't be merged. GitHub has[three merge methods](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/pull-request-merges) , and the repository settings decide which ones are allowed:


Method


What lands on the base branch


GitHub suggests it when


Create a merge commit


All the branch's commits, plus a merge commit


Complete history matters, or each commit is meaningful on its own


Squash and merge


One commit that combines the whole pull request


The pull request is one logical change, especially with many small fixup commits


Rebase and merge


Each commit added onto the base branch, with no merge commit


You want a linear history and the commits are already organized clearly


Rebase and merge always creates new commit SHAs and updates the committer information, unlike a plain` git rebase` onto an ancestor commit. Squash and merge builds a default commit message you can edit, and depending on your settings it can include the pull request title, so the title can end up as the commit message on your main branch. If your team follows Conventional Commits, a format where each commit message starts with a type such as` feat:` or` fix:` , write pull request titles the same way.


GitHub can also take the waiting out of merging:


-


**Auto-merge**[merges a pull request](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/automatically-merging-a-pull-request) on its own once all required reviews and status checks pass. A repository has to enable it first, and` gh pr merge --auto` turns it on from the terminal.


-


**A merge queue**[automates merges](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue) into a busy branch and makes sure incompatible changes never break it, without each author having to update their branch and wait for checks. It's available in public repositories owned by organizations, and in private organization repositories on GitHub Enterprise Cloud. The[GitHub merge queue guide](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/github-merge-queue) covers setup and the CI changes it needs.


### Close or revert


If a change isn't needed anymore, close the pull request without merging it. If you opened it against the wrong base branch, change the base branch instead of closing it and opening a new one. After a merge, you can delete the head branch, and GitHub retargets any open pull requests that used it as their base.


If a merged pull request causes a problem, the **Revert** button near the bottom of the pull request[creates a new pull request](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/reverting-a-pull-request) that reverts the original merge commit.


## How to open a pull request on GitHub


If you don't have write access to a repository, fork it first and open the pull request from a branch in your fork.


### In the browser


These steps follow GitHub's guide to[creating a pull request](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/create-pull-requests/creating-a-pull-request) :


1.


Push your branch to GitHub.


2.


On the repository's main page, pick your branch from the **Branch** menu, then click **Compare & pull request** in the yellow banner.


3.


Set the base branch (where the changes should go) and the compare branch (where you made them).


4.


Write a title and a description.


5.


Click **Create pull request** . For a draft, open the dropdown, select **Create draft pull request** , then click **Draft pull request** .


6.


Ask for reviews from the **Reviewers** section of the sidebar.


### With the GitHub CLI


The GitHub CLI,` gh` , does the same from a terminal. A typical run:


```text
git   switch  -c   fix-login-redirect
# make your changes, then commit and push them
git   add .
git   commit  -m    "Fix redirect loop after login"
git   push  -u   origin fix-login-redirect


gh pr create  --base   main  --title    "Fix redirect loop after login"   \
--body    "Fixes #123"    --reviewer   monalisa  --draft
```


```text
git   switch  -c   fix-login-redirect
# make your changes, then commit and push them
git   add .
git   commit  -m    "Fix redirect loop after login"
git   push  -u   origin fix-login-redirect


gh pr create  --base   main  --title    "Fix redirect loop after login"   \
--body    "Fixes #123"    --reviewer   monalisa  --draft
```


```text
git   switch  -c   fix-login-redirect
# make your changes, then commit and push them
git   add .
git   commit  -m    "Fix redirect loop after login"
git   push  -u   origin fix-login-redirect


gh pr create  --base   main  --title    "Fix redirect loop after login"   \
--body    "Fixes #123"    --reviewer   monalisa  --draft
```


`[gh pr create](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_create)` prints the new pull request's URL. A few flags worth knowing:


-


` --fill` fills the title and body from your commit messages.


-


` --draft` opens the pull request as a draft.


-


` --reviewer` requests reviews from people or teams.


-


` --web` opens the browser so you can finish there.


If you leave out` --title` and` --body` ,` gh` prompts for them, and if your branch isn't pushed yet, it asks where to push it. Once the pull request is open:


```text
gh pr checks  --watch                      # follow CI until it finishes
gh pr ready                             # mark the draft ready for review
gh pr merge  --squash    --delete  -branch      # squash, merge, delete the branch
```


```text
gh pr checks  --watch                      # follow CI until it finishes
gh pr ready                             # mark the draft ready for review
```


```text
gh pr checks  --watch                      # follow CI until it finishes
gh pr ready                             # mark the draft ready for review
```


Without a pull request number, these commands act on the pull request for your current branch.`[gh pr merge](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_merge)` also takes` --merge` or` --rebase` for the other two methods.


## How to make a pull request easy to review


### Keep it small and focused


GitHub's guide to[helping others review your changes](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/concepts/helping-others-review-your-changes) says "Small, focused pull requests are easier to review and safer to merge." Google's[code review guide](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html) , where a CL (changelist) is a change under review, says "100 lines is usually a reasonable size for a CL, and 1000 lines is usually too large." It adds that small changes are reviewed more quickly and more thoroughly and are less likely to introduce bugs, and that refactoring belongs in a separate change from feature work or bug fixes. Our post on[the ideal PR size](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/does-pr-size-actually-matter) covers what large pull requests cost and how to split them.


When a change can't be small,[stacked pull requests](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/stacked-pull-requests) split it into a chain of pull requests where each one builds on the one below, so reviewers see one layer at a time. GitHub's own[stacked pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/get-started/about-stacked-prs) became generally available on October 6, 2026.


### Write the description for someone who wasn't there


Say what changed, why, and where reviewers should look first. Google's guide to[CL descriptions](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/cl-descriptions.html) asks for a first line that's "a short summary of specifically what is being done," followed by context such as why the change is being made. Add how you tested it, screenshots for UI changes, and a closing keyword for the issue. For example:

### Review your own diff first


Before you request review, read your own diff the way a reviewer would. GitHub's docs suggest checking for accidental changes and making sure the relevant builds and tests have run. A comment on lines that need context saves the reviewer a question.


### Make the state obvious


Keep unfinished work in draft, and use labels to show whether a pull request is ready for review, blocked or still in progress. After you address feedback, re-request review from the same reviewer with the button next to their name in the Reviewers sidebar.


For more on cutting the time pull requests spend waiting, see[how to speed up PR reviews on GitHub](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/how-to-speed-up-pr-reviews-on-github) .


### Read AI-written code before you ask for review


If a coding agent wrote the change, read the whole diff yourself before you request review. Otherwise the reviewer may be the first person who reads it.


AI-written code still has bugs.[Bug Bench](https://www.cubic.dev/bugbench) , our public benchmark, counts a bug when a developer upvotes a cubic review finding on AI-written code or an AI coding agent addresses it. Every one of the 7 ranked models has counted bugs, with relative bug rates from 0.65 (GPT-5.6 Sol) to 1.50 (Claude Opus 5.5), where 1.00 is the average across all AI-attributed lines. The data is observational: teams choose their models, so a rate reflects the code each model was used for as well as the model.


An AI reviewer such as cubic reviews pull requests on GitHub, finds bugs and learns your team's rules, so with[AI code review](https://www.cubic.dev/ai-code-review) your teammates start from a first pass.


## FAQ


### Why do we use pull requests?


A pull request gets a change reviewed before it reaches the main branch, gives the team one place to discuss it, and keeps a record of who approved what. Branch rules can require approvals and passing status checks, so changes to a protected branch can be required to go through review.


### What is the difference between a PR and an MR?


Only the name. GitHub and Bitbucket call it a pull request (PR), and GitLab calls it a merge request (MR). The features around it differ, such as how each platform handles drafts, approval rules and merge queues.


### Why is it called a pull request?


Because you're asking the people who own the target branch to pull your commits into it. The term comes from git, where` git pull` fetches changes from another repository or branch and integrates them into the current branch. A merge is the git operation that combines the two branches, and merging the pull request is what runs it once the request is accepted.


### How do I check my pull requests?


On GitHub, go to[github.com/pulls](https://github.com/pulls) to see your pull requests. From a terminal,` gh pr status` shows the status of the pull requests relevant to you, and` gh pr list --author "@me"` lists the open pull requests you created in the current repository.


### What is a pull request vs a commit?


A commit is a saved change to one or more files, which git records with a unique ID along with who made it and when. A pull request is a request on GitHub to merge the commits on one branch into another, with review, discussion and checks around it. One pull request usually holds several commits, and squash and merge turns them into a single commit.
